summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under Brazil's national framework. The state is assessed at the national score: no deviation from the national position has been identified that is material enough to score separately (within ±0.02). A visitor to Curitiba or anywhere else in the state faces the same law as a visitor to any other part of the country.

Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds all civil registries after a 14-1 vote, and adoption rights have followed since 2015. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Explicit national discrimination protections have rested on that ruling since 2019. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute sits alongside it and that repeal efforts are before Congress.

In 2023 the Superior Court of Justice allowed nonbinary people to amend their civil records, a document rule that operates in Paraná as elsewhere in Brazil. Intersex people have no specific protections in Brazilian law.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's 2026 overview records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. Recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; placement is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision taken after the person has been consulted about their preference, with female, male and LGBTI-specific units set out and the declared preference recorded. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, documenting housing in units operated as masculine and treating placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.
tangentialFactors:
Courts have applied the post-2019 provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Targeted violence against LGBTIQ people persists in settings a visitor may use. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists.

Official hostility and mobilisation run alongside the protections. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of Brazil and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Sub-national variation exists within the national framework. A 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law grants parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine. No equivalent Paraná-specific instrument is recorded in the sources.
localsOnly:
LGB people serve openly in the Brazilian military, and explicit national discrimination protections have been in force since 2019.

Residents may amend civil records to a nonbinary marker under the Superior Court of Justice's 2023 allowance, and gender change has required no surgery since the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2018 ruling.

Extension of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women would bring residents within the country's violence-prevention statutes; the 2022 case law shows lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward that outcome.

Adoption rights have been available to same-sex couples since 2015, and the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Paraná-specific enforcement record is sourced: the inventory contains no prosecutions, police practice or judicial decisions from the state of Paraná itself, so state-level application of the 2019 provisions remains unresolved rather than absent.

The status of the repeal efforts before Congress noted in the March 2026 overview is unresolved in the sources; no date, sponsor or outcome is given.

Whether Paraná's own legislature or executive has issued state-level anti-discrimination or housing instruments comparable to Rio de Janeiro's 2015 law is not sourced here.

The divergence between Resolution 348/366 and prison practice is documented for Rio de Janeiro state only; equivalent census data for Paraná's prison system is not available in the inventory.
